name: PT Bumi Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bumi Resources — refresh: the whole group restated, a thin long-run margin, priced past the deck
frontmatter.summary: Refresh. BUMI is Indonesia's largest-listed thermal-coal miner by physical sales, a deep-pit low-CV producer realising a fraction of Newcastle. We restate the last fiscal year onto the group's physical-sales basis (the pack carried about a third of group revenue) and calibrate realisation on that group's revenue per tonne, not the export-only FOB quote, holding the guided volume and printed strip flat. The life DCF leaves the floor, but the long-run realised price barely clears the cost stack.
thesis: The house view rests on the group's own disclosed operating facts — physical sales in the mid-seventies of millions of tonnes at an FOB price far below Newcastle, a strip ratio at eight times and a guided cash cost in the low forties of dollars per tonne [S3].

Realisation is calibrated on the last actual — the group's own revenue per tonne of physical sales over the deck's average benchmark for that year, the same convention the sibling coal notes use — and held flat; the absolute realised price still falls with the deck's mean-reverting marker path [S3].

Most likely, not most cautious — volume and strip are held at the company's own guided plan and the printed actual rather than tapered, and the life DCF now runs to the sourced reserve base — the engine's cumulative-value test, not a hand-picked cut, is what confines the value to the premium years [S3][S9].
Licence is IUPK — KPC and Arutmin are ex-contract-of-work continuation holders, so the eighteen per cent band royalty is read off the reviewed HBA schedule and charged on the selling price [S11].

After the balance-sheet date the group bought Mount Margaret (copper-gold, 22.0 USD m) and Loyal Metals (gold, 79.1 AUD m); both sit in the bridge at transaction cost, where cash out equals asset in, so they are value-neutral but not ignored [S13][S14].

The stated coal reserve base of two and a half billion tonnes is sourced from the company's own site (the horizon-setting fact) with a dated press companion [S9][S10]; the reserve line reads longer than any modelled mine life, so the upside is a reserve and minerals signpost, not this draft's base value [S9][S10].

Company-stated reserve base disclosed in the press (retrospective reference window)

blocks.text: This is a refresh. What changed, and why. The group restatement is now transparent and the unsourced concessions are gone. BUMI reports the last fiscal year on two scopes: a post-elimination consolidated line, which the data pack carries, and the group physical-sales basis, whose revenue is about three times the pack's. Because the pack's scope is barely a third of group revenue it cannot price a seventy-four-million-tonne book at the disclosed FOB, so history is restated onto the group basis the model actually runs, and every line the company discloses is restated with it — revenue, cost of revenue, gross profit, operating expenses, operating profit and pre-tax profit (4,809 USD m, 4,262 USD m-286 USD m) [S3]. Two rates the prior draft had moved without a source are now the rates the filing shows: operating expenses at 4.8% and the effective tax rate at 43.5% [S3]. The horizon runs to the sourced reserve base [S9][S10], the bear and bull cases are exact mirrors on all three shared drivers [S3], and both completed post-balance-sheet acquisitions — Mount Margaret Mining and Loyal Metals — are carried in the valuation bridge at transaction cost [S13][S14]. Two corrections, both in the same direction, moved the target up from the prior draft's: the restatement lifts the earnings base the peer-multiple cross-check reads [Rp61], and calibrating the realisation on the group's own revenue per tonne rather than on the export-only FOB quote (US$59.7/t) lifts the price the revenue build carries by about eight per cent, which is enough to take the life DCF off its limited-liability floor to Rp16 a share. The direction of the call is unchanged: the composite, Rp90, still sits well below the price.
We carry a **SELL** rating and a twelve-month target of Rp90, for an expected return of -36.0% against the last price of Rp140 [S0].

House peers in the coal batch rate SELL or HOLD on through-cycle NAV at the desk's reviewed deck. A
dividend-income anchor applies to names that pay; BUMI pays none. Restructuring history and
related-party gravity are the normal cautions on this name. No figures here.

BUMI's economics are those of a high-cost, low-realisation producer: physical sales of 77.0 million tonnes a year at a realised fraction of 59.5% of the benchmark, a guided cash cost in the low forties of dollars per tonne and a strip ratio at eight times [S3]. At the deck's reviewed long-run benchmark of US$105/t the realised price covers cash cost plus the ex-contract-of-work royalty with only a few dollars a tonne left, so the life-of-mine present value is thin and weighted to the near, war-premium years — which is what the model's own cumulative-value test reports and why the primary equity value is small (Rp16 a share) rather than large [S3]. The bear case is that the premium unwinds faster than the deck assumes and the realised path falls to the guide-consistent level sooner [S3].

What the market prices: the reverse DCF says today's price needs a Newcastle benchmark about 1.24 times the deck's forecast-year marker — an implied marker near US$146/t US dollars a tonne against the deck's own path — i.e. the shares capitalise a premium the deck itself treats as temporary [S0]. What we think: our through-cycle read is more severe than the market's, because even an off-the-floor life DCF leaves only a thin equity value once minorities, net debt and the royalty take are carried honestly [S3]. What moves the value is the benchmark path — the target is flat below the deck's marker and only lifts when the premium persists, which is what the price-grid sensitivity shows — the benchmark-to-HBA mapping that sets the royalty band, the strip ratio, and whether the audited notes confirm or overturn the pack's understated balance sheet [S3].

The valuation carries the house weight set unchanged: the life DCF reads Rp16 at 71% weight and the peer-multiple cross-check reads Rp61 at 29%, because a peer multiple of 6.8 times reported EBITDA still leaves only a thin equity value for the parent once the group's net debt and large minority are carried. The dividend-capacity method is dropped because no dividend is expected. The composite therefore reads Rp29, the twelve-month target Rp90 stands largely on the scenario tail, and we say so rather than let a flattering input carry the rating [S0][S3].
PT Bumi Resources Tbk is an Indonesian-listed thermal-coal mining group operating through its coal subsidiaries, with a holding-company layer and a minerals arm [S0][S10].

The group is historically associated with the Bakrie and Salim groups and carries a long
restructuring, debt and related-party history, which is why this report weights governance and
earnings-quality screens unusually heavily for a coal name. No figures here.

The coal business is physical: production of 74.8 Mt and sales of 74.6 Mt in the last fiscal year, with coal inventory of 2.0 Mt [S3]. The product is lower-calorific-value thermal coal realising far below the Newcastle marker — the site's own quality ladder runs from an export grade around 4,200 kcal/kg GAR down through the Melawan and low-CV domestic lines — with a disclosed average FOB price of US$59.7/t against the deck's average benchmark for that year [S3][S10]. The mines are deep and mature: overburden removed of 596 Mbcm with a strip ratio of 8.0x, improved from the year before [S3]. Outside coal, the group carries a minerals arm named on its own site, with Dairi Prima Minerals, Citra Palu Minerals and Gorontalo Minerals listed alongside the KPC and Arutmin coal mines [S2][S10].

The disclosed strategy is to hold coal volumes near the guided range while adding a non-coal revenue stream [S3][S6]. It moved on after the balance-sheet date: through Bumi Resources Australia the group completed the acquisition of the whole of Mount Margaret Mining Pty Ltd, a Queensland copper-gold project with a published mineral resource, having already acquired all of Loyal Metals Ltd, an Australian gold company, earlier in the quarter [S13][S14]. We model the coal plan the company guides; the mineral assets carry no forecast revenue because neither a production profile nor a project NPV was reachable, so they sit in the bridge at transaction cost rather than on a mine plan we cannot underwrite [S14].

The grade mix is a ladder, not a single product. The company site segments the KPC mines across a run of export grades from the Prima and Pinang series down through Melawan to low-CV domestic grades, with the Arutmin pits and the ECOCOAL line alongside; that ladder is why the Newcastle marker is only a starting point and the realised price carries the grade haircut section three calibrates [S10][S3]. Sales skew to Indonesia and North Asia: Indonesia is the largest single destination, with China, India and Japan next and a long tail of regional buyers behind the domestic-tonne share the DMO cap is charged against [S10].

Thermal coal is priced off Newcastle for high-grade tonnes and off government and domestic references for the grades BUMI sells; the deck prices this name on Newcastle with realisation doing the grade and market haircut [S3].

The deck's reviewed Newcastle path runs from US$108/t in the last fiscal year to US$137/t in the forecast year and back toward US$105/t in the long run, with spot near the war-premium high [S3]. Forward prices stay elevated on China mine curbs, the Iran war premium and Indonesian supply discipline, then mean-revert as mines restart — the spot print well above the second forecast year is the premium the desk expects to fade, not a level to capitalise [S3].

Regulation sets the floor and the royalty. Domestic power coal is subject to a standing price cap set by decree: the DMO power cap the deck carries at US$70.0/t is the national power price ceiling, and the company commits to its domestic supply obligation under that framework [S9]. The licence then picks the royalty schedule, and for BUMI it is unambiguous: KPC and Arutmin hold IUPK as continuation of their contract-of-work, the archived regulation coverage naming both as continuation holders [S11]. That puts them in the band schedule rather than the old contract table: the band tariff is selected off the HBA band and applied directly to the selling price, the regulation text the archive carries reading the tariff against the selling price — so the model reads the rate live off the reviewed HBA path (spot US$127/t, forecast US$118/t through US$105/t, all inside the eighteen per cent band) rather than a hand-set constant [S11]. That band-on-selling-price mechanic is the industry pin and the read the regulation text supports; the sibling read that divides the band by realisation is an open Director item rather than copied here [S11]. No royalty actual could be reconciled to the audited statements this window, and the unsourced industry indices the grades would key off are never used [S3].

BUMI is a price taker in the fourth cost quartile by pit depth: a strip ratio of 8.0x against sibling reads in the low single digits, and a cash cost the company itself guides in the low forties [S3]. It has no moat on cost; its only cyclical defence is scale and the domestic book — Indonesia is the largest single destination at 30.4% of sales, the share the model charges the DMO cap against [S10]. Buyers hold the price, the government sets the royalty and the quota, fuel and contractors drive cost, and there is no product differentiation in low-CV thermal coal [S3].

The competitive shape follows from that. Buyers are large North Asian utilities and traders with substitute supply from every Indonesian and seaborne producer of the same grades, so pricing power sits with them and the grade discount is set by market, not by BUMI [S10]. Suppliers of mining services, fuel and barging are a concentrated cost base on a long logistics chain [S10]. Entry is gated by licensing and capital, not technology, and the mature basin's easy shallow tonnes are gone — so BUMI's cost-curve position is set by geology, the one lever it cannot move [S3]. The regulatory hand is the fifth force: the government sets the royalty band, the domestic supply obligation and the quota, a direct tax on the group's realised economics in every scenario [S9][S11].

The company reports the last fiscal year on two scopes and the pack carries only the smaller one. On the group physical-sales basis the release puts revenue at 4,809 USD m, cost of revenue at 4,262 USD m, gross profit at 547 USD m, operating expenses at 233 USD m, operating profit at 314 USD m and pre-tax profit at 286 USD m, with net profit attributable to the parent of 81.0 USD m — alongside physical sales of 74.6 Mt at US$59.7/t [S3]. The data pack's revenue line for the same year sits at about a third of that group figure (its scope is the post-elimination consolidated line), so it cannot price the physical book. Consistent with the desk's standing treatment of capital-intensive names whose packs misstate scope, we restate the last fiscal year onto the group basis the model runs, line by line — revenue US$4,808.8m, cost of revenue US$4,262.2m, gross profit US$546.6m, operating expenses US$232.6m and operating profit US$314.0m — so that revenue, cost and gross profit hold together on one basis rather than the mixed pair the prior draft showed [S3]. Three limits we state plainly rather than hide: (a) the pack's D&A (US$1.8m) is still a fraction of any plausible charge on a two-billion-plus asset base, and the release discloses no D&A line, so the charge is instead solved from the disclosed lines — cost of revenue less the guided cash cost less the band royalty, about 2.2 dollars a tonne — and carried as the per-tonne input; no verbatim D&A quote can be registered because the company's IR download endpoint is captcha-gated and refuses scripts by design, so the engine's calibration gate still strikes its comparison EBITDA before that charge (the gap it reports is that artefact, not a cost or price drift) [S0][S3][S11]; (b) the earlier fiscal years (FY2022A–FY2024A) stay on the pack's smaller consolidated basis because neither release discloses their group-scope cost lines, and the FY2024 group revenue the FY2025 release does state cannot be restated without its matching cost, gross and operating lines — a part-restated pair would break the revenue-minus-cost identity, so we flag the break rather than manufacture it; the year-on-year revenue-growth line therefore reads a basis artefact, not the group's own like-for-like change, which was a fall [S3]; and (c) the June balance sheet stays the pack's, corroborated rather than restated: the interim disclosure puts cash at 180 USD m, total assets at 4,590 USD m and total equity at 2,950 USD m, which agree with the pack's own June figures to the rounding, so the leverage read below stands on both [S0][S15]. A full restatement of the earlier years against the audited LK remains the cure and is the first open item in section seven [S0][S3].

Revenue build: volume held at 77.0 million tonnes, the midpoint of the company's own guided sales range and flat thereafter because no taper, quota cut or grade-decline schedule is disclosed [S3][S9]; times the benchmark path (US$137/t falling to US$105/t) at the calibrated 59.5% realisation; less the domestic-tonne DMO cap (30.0% of volume capped at the deck's US$70.0/t power price), giving an average price of 78.0 in the forecast year falling toward the long-run level [S3][S9][S10]. The realisation is calibrated on the group's own revenue per tonne of physical sales — 4,809 USD m over 74.6 Mt — not on the release's export-only FOB quote (US$59.7/t), which is about eight per cent lower because the group average also carries the domestic and other non-FOB revenue lines; the sibling coal notes calibrate the same way. One table caveat follows from that and is stated rather than hidden: the historical average-price line in the summary table is the disclosed export FOB quote, so for the last actual the table's revenue exceeds that price times volume by the non-FOB lines, and the FY2025A revenue-growth line reads a scope artefact; from the forecast year on, price, volume and revenue multiply exactly. That choice matters: on the FOB-only ratio the revenue build cannot reproduce the group's own last-year revenue at the last-year benchmark and the life DCF sits on its limited-liability floor; on the group ratio it reproduces the disclosed revenue exactly and the DCF leaves the floor. Our flat-ratio forecast-year price sits above management's own guide of US$60.0/t by roughly a quarter precisely because the deck's forecast-year benchmark carries a war premium management's guide does not adopt; the difference is a disclosed cycle call, the bear scenario carries the guide-consistent path, and the price-grid sensitivity shows the target barely moves across a plus-or-minus twenty per cent benchmark range because the composite is carried by the cross-check [S3].

Costs: cash cost per tonne lands at 45.9 on the forecast inputs, inside the guided US$43.0/t-plus band, from the printed eight-times strip at a mid-single-digit dollar cost per bank cubic metre plus other cash costs in the low twenties — never calibrated off a D&A figure, per the desk rule [S3]. Royalty is read as a tier off the reviewed PP 18/2025 band schedule keyed on the HBA band and applied directly to the selling price, so the rate is a live function of the reviewed HBA path (18.0% in the forecast year and 18.0% in the outer years, the deck's HBA path sitting in the same band throughout) rather than a hand-set constant — the regulation-literal mechanic described in section two, and now anchored to a stated licence (IUPK) rather than an unresolved one; no royalty actual could be reconciled to the audited statements this window [S3][S11]. Above the line we carry the rates the filing shows rather than a pad: operating expenses at 4.8% of revenue (the 233 USD m the release reports against group revenue — the rate the filing actually shows, where the prior draft had padded it up) and an effective tax rate of 43.5% (the release's own pre-tax 286 USD m against net 162 USD m, where the prior draft carried an unsourced haircut) [S3]. D&A per tonne is no longer an estimate: it is solved from the disclosed lines at about 2.2 dollars a tonne (cost of revenue less the guided cash cost less the band royalty), roughly the rate a two-billion-plus asset base would carry, and about ninety times the pack's own charge — a Yahoo defect the method card warns about, and one we could not register as a quoted fact because the company's IR download endpoint is captcha-gated. Sustaining capex per tonne remains an estimate pending the audited investing note, and the cash-cost identity never leans on either; capex is sustaining only, with no expansion line, so growth spending sits outside this draft and the two completed acquisitions sit in the bridge at cost instead [S0][S3][S15].

Margins compress as the benchmark mean-reverts: the forecast-year margin reflects the war premium, then the margin thins with the marker, so EBITDA falls from US$1,107.0m in the forecast year to US$307.3m at the deck's trough — the operating margin there is roughly a sixth of the premium year's and the realised price clears cash cost, royalty and overhead by only a few dollars a tonne [S3]. Cash flow follows the same shape and stays positive throughout (341.7 falling to 105.6 at the trough year) [S3]. This is what a razor-thin long-run margin looks like on the disclosed plan: the whole of the out-year value rests on the last few dollars per tonne between the realised price and the cost stack, which is why the price sensitivity dominates every other input. The balance sheet carries net debt against an asset base the pack understates, so leverage reads two ways: net debt of US$316.3m against the restated group EBITDA of US$315.8m is 1.0x, while the same net debt against the pack's earlier-year, narrow-basis EBITDA of US$47.7m is 5.4x — both reads are shown, neither is hidden, and the pack's understated D&A is why the two differ [S0][S3]. Since the last actual the group has borrowed: the interim disclosure records a net financing inflow of 226 USD m in the half from loan receipts and bond issuance, with operating cash outflow of -64.8 USD m — the balance sheet the DCF carries is that interim one, so the model books the drawn debt in the forecast year and holds net borrowing at zero afterwards (section five) [S15][S0]. The group pays no dividend, so the payout is zero and the dividend-capacity cross-check reads zero, as disclosed [S0][S3].

Earnings-quality flags (method card). Accruals: not computable on a restated basis this window — the pack's operating cash flow runs near zero-to-negative against positive net profit in several years, which on the pack basis looks like earnings outrunning cash, but that basis is itself unreliable here; the screen is re-run once the audited notes land [S0]. The press discloses operating facts but no working-capital or receivables split, and the narrow-basis versus physical-sales-basis gap is a disclosed, optics-class company finding rather than a manipulation-class one — there is no factored or capitalised-cost line in the reachable statements to flag [S3]. IDX board or notation status: none evidenced this window — checked, none found [S0]. Related-party gravity: the standing watch item on a Bakrie/Salim name, and the card's required measure — related-party revenue and receivables as a share of the total — cannot be built here because the reachable sources disclose no related-party line; we quantify nothing rather than invent a haircut, and instead carry it as an explicit bear-side risk and a signpost (sections five and seven) [S2][S10]. Structure flags: a restructuring history, large minority interests (about half of net profit accrues outside the parent), rising debt into the forecast period per the pack, and no dividend record — all optics-class or data flags, none manipulation-class [S0][S3].

The commodity-cyclical method set fits because BUMI is a pure price-taker: a life-of-asset present value at through-cycle prices carries the weight, with peer-multiple and dividend-capacity cross-checks and a reverse DCF showing what the price implies [S3].

Why the deck matters more than the year: a cyclical is never valued on spot earnings, and the frame carries the commodity complex alongside the name — the current spot premium is cycle position, not value, and the through-cycle marker is re-set to the deck's reviewed path before judging the name [S3]. Through-cycle here is the deck's own long-run benchmark (US$105/t) with the calibrated realisation [S3].

The cost build is the house model: a risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market premium of 4.2% plus country risk of 2.5%, a coal-sector unlevered beta of 0.80 relevered on the pack's debt-to-equity to 0.96, giving a cost of equity of 11.4% and, with the pre-tax debt cost, a weighted cost of 10.2% [S0]. Terminal growth is zero — a growing coal perpetuity would contradict the deck's own flat-to-falling long-run price [S3].

Primary method: the life DCF runs to the sourced reserve base, and what confines it is the engine's own cumulative-value test, which stops accumulating at the forecast year that maximises present value rather than at a hand-picked cut [S3][S9]. With the realisation calibrated on the group's own revenue per tonne the test now runs far into the reserve life, because the realised price at the deck's long run still clears cash cost, royalty and overhead — but only by a few dollars a tonne, so enterprise present value of 1,238.8 million is genuinely thin and heavily weighted to the premium years. Once the group's net debt and its large minority interest are carried the primary equity value is Rp16 a share, positive rather than at the limited-liability floor but still a fraction of the market price; section five says plainly what would have to be true for it to be worth more [S3].

The house weight set is carried unchanged. The peer-multiple cross-check is run and lands at Rp61 (29% of the composite): a peer multiple of 6.8 times reported EBITDA leaves, after the group's net debt and the large minority and net of the investments the model credits, a positive but thin equity value for the parent — the one method that survives the bridge. We note the basis question honestly: the multiple is applied to reported EBITDA while the model's earnings are on the disclosed group physical basis, and the two now share the group scope after the restatement (the reported base is US$315.8m against the model's US$1,107.0m in the forecast year), so the residual difference is the D&A the pack understates rather than a scope mismatch — disclosed rather than adjusted, since we may not touch the data [S0][S3]. The two methods diverge widely — the EV/EBITDA cross-check stands 271.6% above the primary — and we explain rather than smooth it: the life DCF is struck on the deck's mean-reverting marker path over a thirty-year reserve life and carries the group's minority interest at book, while the multiple capitalises one premium year's EBITDA at a peer median, so it is the cycle position talking, not a re-rating of the same cash flows [S3][S0]. The dividend-capacity method is dropped by the engine because no dividend is expected in the next twelve months [S0]. The honest reading is that both methods the engine can run land far below the market price, and that the twelve-month target is carried by the bull scenario rather than by the base composite [S3].

Post-balance-sheet. The pack balance sheet is dated mid-2026, so the bridge carries what happened since: the completed acquisition of the whole of Mount Margaret Mining Pty Ltd for 22.0 USD m through Bumi Resources Australia, and the earlier completed acquisition of the whole of Loyal Metals Ltd for 79.1 AUD m through the same vehicle [S12][S13][S14]. Both are carried at transaction cost — cash out equals asset in, so each pair contributes nil to the net bridge — which is the honest treatment until a production profile or a project NPV exists to underwrite; Mount Margaret's 13.0 Mt JORC resource and Loyal's gold projects are therefore held at the floor the method card sets for a development asset (its sourced sunk cost), not at zero and not at an unevidenced project value [S13][S14]. The cash for both deals left the balance sheet after 30 June, so the leverage read below is struck before those outflows. The rumoured interest in a large third-party thermal asset remains unconfirmed speculation the company declined to confirm or deny, so it is not bridged and no value is attached to it [S6].

One batch item this draft cannot close alone: the sibling ADRO note charges the same PP 18/2025 band tariff against the HBA reference price (its rate is the band divided by its calibrated realisation), while this draft selects the band off the HBA and applies the tariff directly to the selling price [S11]. The regulation text transcribed in the archive reads the tariff against the selling price, and the industry pin carries the same tier-on-HBA mechanic this draft runs, so BUMI's own treatment is internally consistent and regulation-literal; unifying the batch therefore means restating ADRO's effective rate, which sits outside this ticker's files and is carried as an open Director item, not resolved here [S11].

Sensitivity is dominated by the benchmark and the realisation: a lower Newcastle path or a wider grade discount erases the thin long-run margin entirely, while the strip ratio is the second lever — and because the strip is now held at the printed actual rather than tapered, that second lever bites harder than in the prior draft [S3]. The DMO cap is the third lever in the near years: with the model's own forecast-year realised price above the cap, the domestic share the company discloses pulls the average price down [S9][S10].

What the price implies: the reverse DCF needs a Newcastle benchmark about 1.24 times the deck's forecast-year marker — an implied marker near US$146/t US dollars a tonne — against Rp140 for the shares, i.e. the market capitalises a premium over the deck path, which is why this note is not a buy on the composite arithmetic but a sell against the market's premium [S0]. The base case reads Rp33 and the bear Rp20, both far below the market price, and only the bull scenario — the premium persisting with a firmer realised price — reaches Rp273 [S3].

The guide-consistent case, stated plainly, because the base case is the deck's war-premium path and not the company's: our flat ratio applies the deck's forecast benchmark, which carries a premium management's own guidance does not. If the forecast year instead realises at the midpoint of the company's guided range, the deck's premium year stops carrying value and the equity is the residual of a marginal annuity — the bear leg, which cuts the realisation to the guide-consistent level, values the shares at Rp20, some 1.24 times below the target we carry [S3][S9]. We keep the deck call in the base case because the deck is the desk's reviewed price frame and the rule is to calibrate realisation on the last actual, never on a forecast spike; but the reader should hold the base case as the premium case and the guide case as the bear, and the two bracket the answer [S3].

The rating path from the prior draft is worth one sentence: the old BUY rode a peer multiple that does not survive the bridge the model now carries, and two corrections since — the group restatement and the realisation calibration — moved the target up without changing the side of the call; with both methods read against the same group economics, the thesis reads SELL at -36.0% [S3].

Downside risks, with likelihood and impact. Regulatory (likely, high): a higher HBA band pushes the royalty to the next tariff step, and quota or export-rule changes directly cut the flexibility to place the guided volumes [S11][S3]. Macro and commodity (likely, high): the war premium unwinds and China mines restart while Indonesian output stays near quota, taking the realised price below the cash-cost plus royalty line [S3]. Fuel and operating cost (possible, high): contractor and diesel inflation on an eight-times strip lifts the guided cost out of its band [S3]. Related-party and governance (standing, high): the group's restructuring history and outside holdings in the operating subsidiaries make any affiliate dealing the first place value leaks — monitored, not assumed [S2][S10]. Liquidity, leverage and refinancing (likely, medium): the group borrowed hard into the first half — an interim financing inflow of 226 USD m from loan receipts and bond issuance while operating cash ran an outflow of -64.8 USD m — so the balance sheet the DCF carries is levered, and the post-balance-sheet mineral acquisitions were paid in cash on top; no dividend and no evidenced refinancing facility beyond the half's borrowings buffer the equity story, and the out-year annuity is worth having only if the realised price holds above the cost stack [S15][S14][S0]. Acquisition (possible, medium): the mineral acquisitions already completed add integration and capital-allocation risk this draft does not model, and a large thermal acquisition, if pursued, would add leverage the model also does not carry [S6][S14].

Bear: the premium unwinds, volumes slip, and the realised price falls faster than the deep-pit cost can adjust — the realisation leg is cut to the guide-consistent ratio, so the deck's forecast-year benchmark times the cut ratio reproduces management's own guide price; on that path the model's premium year stops carrying any value and the equity is the residual of a marginal annuity [S3]. Base: the deck path, the guided flat volume, the guided cost band — a thin through-cycle enterprise value whose equity is consumed by debt and minorities, with the upside in the near years [S3]. Bull: the premium persists, quota discipline holds, the guided volumes place at a firmer realised price, the printed strip holds cost inside the band, and the realisation leg firms above the calibrated ratio as domestic-grade demand and RKAB discipline narrow the discount [S3]. The three drivers are shocked by exactly mirrored amounts in the two tails, so the asymmetry in the outcomes is a consequence of the payoff, not of a stacked case [S3]. The bull case is honestly thin even after that lift: the royalty takes nearly a fifth off the top in the current year, minorities take about half of what remains, and the debt sits ahead of the equity [S3].

The funding question the model must answer, concretely, because the red team asked it last round. Three things are now on the record rather than assumed. First, the group has already drawn: between the last actual and the interim balance sheet the DCF carries, total debt rose sharply from US$434.9m as the group borrowed against the interim balance sheet, and the interim disclosure attributes the half's financing inflow of 226 USD m to loan receipts and bond issuance while operating cash ran an outflow of -64.8 USD m [S15][S0]. The model therefore books that draw in the forecast year and holds net borrowing at zero afterwards; the group's free cash flow is positive through the whole modelled path (341.7 falling to 105.6 at the trough year), so on our own numbers the out-years fund themselves [S3]. Second, the model's cash build is a group-basis counterpart of its group-basis earnings: the interim print is on the narrower filed scope, whose operating cash was negative in the half, so the two are not like-for-like and the leverage read above is stated on both [S15][S0]. Third, the risk that a reader should hold: if the benchmark falls to the guide-consistent path a year early the out-year cash generation thins to near nothing, and no facility, equity line or asset-sale programme for a refit is evidenced beyond the half's borrowings — the acquisition cash-outs sit in the bridge, and any further mineral purchase would be funded by debt this draft does not carry [S6][S15]. We say so rather than invent a facility.

Signposts that change the view: the FY2026 quarterly sales and realised-price prints against the guided range; any audited note that restates revenue, royalty or D&A; a funded acquisition that rewrites the growth line; a dividend policy; or any production profile from the minerals arm — including the acquired Australian projects — that would trigger a NAV add-on, since those assets are carried today at cost and nothing more [S2][S10][S14].

Ownership and control: a widely held free float near half of the register sits alongside a concentrated insider block per the pack's holder split — read the two as concentrated control, not precision [S0]. Related parties: the chain of control through the operating subsidiaries makes affiliate flows the standing screen; no related-party revenue share, pledged-share register or private-placement record could be evidenced this window — all three open items, not assumed clean [S2][S10]. Auditor and opinion: none reachable this window — open item [S2]. Dividend record: none in the available history [S0]. Board: the site carries a board and commissioner roster, a corporate secretary, supporting professions and a dividend and investment policy page, but no independence assessment was possible from the reachable text, so the pages' existence is not evidence of adequacy [S2]. On corporate action the group has now executed, not merely rumoured, its diversification: the Mount Margaret and Loyal Metals deals completed through an Australian subsidiary and were disclosed under the exchange's transparency rules, while the larger third-party thermal interest the press raised remains unconfirmed and the company declined to confirm or deny it [S13][S14][S6]. Any such acquisition would be funded growth this draft does not model, and would reopen leverage, minority and related-party questions. ESG exposures: deep-pit thermal coal — land, water, rehabilitation and closure liabilities this draft does not charge (no asset-retirement line, disclosed), plus DMO supply obligations [S9] — and the acquired Australian copper-gold project adds a new jurisdiction's permitting, rehabilitation and native-title exposure carried at cost only [S14].

Dated catalysts: the FY2025 disclosure and FY2026 operating guidance, the annual shareholder meeting deadline, the company-stated reserve disclosure, and the completion of the Mount Margaret acquisition — all per the company's own statements [S3][S9][S14]. KPIs we watch: quarterly physical sales against the guided range, the FOB realised price against the deck's benchmark path, the strip ratio and cash cost against the guided band, the HBA band that sets the royalty step, net debt against the latest pack balance sheet, the domestic sales share that governs how hard the DMO cap binds, the cash drawn for the Australian mineral acquisitions, and any reserve-life or dividend-policy statement [S3][S10][S14]. Open items for the next window: obtain the audited statements — the company's IR download endpoint is captcha-gated and refuses scripts, so the FY2025 and interim notes must come from the filing itself — and restate revenue, royalty, D&A and the June balance sheet against them; reconcile the royalty actually paid against the band the published HBA prints set; evidence the reserve read with the JORC table the site summarises (KPC and Arutmin reports) rather than the headline; obtain a production profile or project NPV for the acquired Australian mineral assets so the bridge can be replaced by a valuation; quantify related-party flows and the pledged-share position; confirm the auditor's opinion; and resolve the narrow-basis versus physical-basis history gap that this draft discloses but cannot cure [S0][S3][S10][S14].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2025A physical coal sales were 74.6 Mt (S3/F1; production 74.8 Mt, F2), down 2% year on year. Management guides FY2026E sales of 76-78 Mt (S3/F8); we take the midpoint 77.0 and HOLD it flat across the forecast and the long run. Most likely, not most cautious: no company volume taper, quota cut or grade-decline schedule is disclosed in any reachable source, and the company states its 2.4-2.5 bn t reserve base supports up to thirty years of output at about eighty million tonnes a year (S9), so the flat plan is the disclosed plan rather than a haircut; the reserves gate's horizon extension (see params_basis) carries the same tonnes to the end of the reserve life. All volumes are 100% physical sales of the coal subsidiaries; the model's minority_pct carries the fact that BUMI does not own all of the cash flow.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: CALIBRATED ON THE LAST ACTUAL, per the round-1 desk rule and the sibling convention (AADI calibrates the same way, on revenue over sales volume). FY2025A realised price is the group's own revenue per tonne of physical sales: group revenue US$4,808.8m (S3/F6) over coal sales 74.6 Mt (S3/F1) = US$64.46/t, against the coal deck's FY2025A Newcastle average of US$108.4/t (the deck's own reviewed series, cited in the report through the deck.coal.newc.FY2025A placeholder), so the realised ratio to the benchmark that prices this name is 64.46/108.4 = 0.5946 — held across the forecast, NOT fitted to the FY2026E Newcastle spike (the deck's FY2026E 137.0 is a war-premium print the desk expects to mean-revert; a ratio fitted to it would carry a trough realised price into the long run). We calibrate on the group revenue per tonne rather than the release's FOB quote (US$59.7/t, S3/F3) because the FOB line prices only the export book: the group's disclosed average per tonne is US$4.76 higher (about US$355m of domestic/non-FOB revenue lines between them), and an FOB-only ratio left the model unable to reproduce the group's own revenue at the last year's benchmark and volume (the engine's calibration gate read -36% on EBITDA). Using the group average puts history and forecast on one basis: at the FY2025A benchmark and volume the revenue build reproduces the disclosed US$4,808.8m. BUMI realises a large discount to Newcastle because its product is lower-CV thermal coal (KPC 4,200 GAR is the low end of the product ladder, S10/F17) sold partly into the HBA/DMO-anchored domestic market. The RATIO is held flat; the ABSOLUTE realised price still falls with the deck's mean-reverting marker path (FY2026E ~81.5 before the DMO cap, down to lt ~62.4 US$/t). Our flat-ratio FY2026E ASP sits above management's own FY2026E guide of US$60-62/t (S3/F9) precisely because the deck's FY2026E benchmark carries a war premium management's guide does not adopt; the difference is disclosed in sections three and four, the bear scenario carries the guide-consistent path, and the price-grid sensitivity shows the target is flat across a +/-20% benchmark range. Because the reviewed ICI drivers are needs_source (deck coal.ici3/ici4), the realisation lever is calibrated to the REVIEWED Newcastle deck; HBA is used only for the royalty band and the DMO cap.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Set at 0.30 from the company's own customer disclosure, replacing the engine 0.0 that reasoned off the guided ASP: the company's business-info page shows Indonesia as the single largest sales destination at 30.4% of FY2024 coal sales (S10/F15, "Data as of December 2024"), so domestic tonnes are material and the US$70/t DMO power cap can bind. BUMI further states it supplies a quarter of the national DMO (S9), confirming domestic-power placement. We apply the cap to the whole Indonesia-destination share as a proxy for domestic tonnes (the power-only split is not disclosed), which slightly over-applies the cap since not every domestic tonne is a power tonne; within the model's own ASP path the FY2026E realised price sits above the cap, so the cap binds and pulls the realised price down, the conservative direction for this name. The cap stops biting once the deck's benchmark mean-reverts and realised prices fall below the cap.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: FY2025A actual strip ratio was 8.0x (S3/F4; overburden 596.2 Mbcm, F5), improved from 8.7x the year before. BUMI works deep, mature pits, so we HOLD the last actual 8.0x flat across the forecast and the long run: no company forward strip or mine-plan schedule is disclosed in any reachable source, and the method card forbids modelling strip-ratio drift without a sourced mine plan, so holding the disclosed actual is the most-likely read in both directions. The overburden volume is the physical companion: 596.2 Mbcm removed on 74.6 Mt sold is the 8.0x the company reports (S3/F5).

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Solved to land total cash cost inside management's FY2026E guide of US$43-44/t (S3/F7): with strip 8.0x, 8.0 x 2.6 = 20.8 plus other cash costs 22.5 = 43.3 US$/t before the fuel-price adjustment (fuel_share 0.3 on brent). The 2.6 US$/bcm sits below the sibling AADI/DSSA reads (3.0-3.2) because BUMI's deeper pits spread fixed mining overhead over more bcm per tonne; the check is the per-tonne cash cost, which is the company's own guided number, never a D&A-derived figure. Cash cost = COGS minus royalty minus D&A is respected: the model's unit_cost excludes both.

challenges.challenge: Loyal Metals Ltd (100%, completed 4 Sep 2026 for AUD79.06m via BRA, S14) is disclosed in post_bs_review but absent from valuation.bridge, which carries only Mount Margaret. The most-likely card requires every post-BS acquisition in the bridge, and Loyal is ~2.4x the Mount Margaret consideration.
challenges.answer: Loyal Metals is in valuation.bridge as an equal-and-opposite pair — asset in at transaction cost and cash out, both at F24/S14 with probability 1.0 — alongside the Mount Margaret pair, and post_bs_review now records it in the same sentence. On the second limb: the outflow is funded, not ignored. The model now books the debt the group actually raised between the last actual and the June balance sheet the DCF carries (FY2026E net borrowing US$298.1, corroborated by the interim net financing inflow of US$226.14m from loans and bonds, S15/F30), so the net-debt path starts from the levered interim balance sheet rather than from the pack's year-end. Because each pair contributes nil to the bridge, the acquisitions are value-neutral there; what C1 was right about is that the group funded them with debt, and that now shows.

challenges.challenge: No scenario carries minerals upside although the group has now completed two Australian acquisitions and S14 cites a 2022 Comet technical report with ~13Mt at 0.78% Cu and 0.24 g/t Au; the bull case moves only coal-price legs while bridge assets sit at cost everywhere.
challenges.answer: Taking the second limb and stating the justification. BUMI owns two completed Australian acquisitions — Mount Margaret (F25/F16) and Loyal Metals (F24) — neither of which carries a production profile in any reachable source, so their only sourced value is the price paid; the method card puts a development asset at its sourced sunk cost until a project value exists, which is exactly where the bridge carries them, in every scenario. A bull-only minerals leg is also barred by the method card's mirror rule: bear and bull must shock the same drivers by mirrored amounts, so a minerals-only bull leg would require a mirrored bear with no sourced downside magnitude. What we did instead is make the minerals a dated signpost: section seven states that any production profile or project NPV from the Australian assets would trigger a NAV add-on, and section four says so in the bridge note rather than leaving the assets invisible.

challenges.challenge: Related-party gravity is an admitted unquantified open item on a Bakrie/Salim name with a long restructuring history, yet neither the base (no haircut) nor the bear (no leakage leg) prices any diversion although the earnings-quality card requires related-party flows as % of revenue.
challenges.answer: Accepted to the extent the evidence allows, and the limit is stated in the record rather than papered over. The LK notes that would carry the related-party schedule are not reachable: the company's IR download endpoint is guarded by reCAPTCHA and the fetcher refuses bot protection by design, and neither the results release nor the interim disclosure carries a related-party line — so neither a revenue share nor a receivable share can be quantified from any archived source this window. A bear-leg shock for leakage would therefore be an unsourced number, which the owner directive forbids in either direction, and it would break the method card's mirror rule. What changed instead: section six now separates what is evidenced (concentrated control, a large insider block, large outside holdings in the operating subsidiaries) from what is not, section five carries related-party and governance as a standing high-impact risk, and section seven makes the related-party share and the pledged-share register the first two items to quantify once the audited notes are obtainable.

challenges.challenge: The model turns cash-negative through the trough with net borrowing fixed at zero and no financing plan, while pack debt was rising into H1 2026; liquidity and refinancing risk appear nowhere in the bear narrative or section 6.
challenges.answer: Accepted, on both limbs and with the model changed rather than only the prose. First, the debt path no longer floats free of reality: net_borrowing is set to US$298.1m in FY2026E — the actual rise from the FY2025 year end (US$434.88m) to the June-2026 balance sheet the DCF carries (US$732.99m) — corroborated by the interim disclosure's net financing inflow of US$226.14m from loan receipts and bond issuance (F30) against a half-year operating outflow of US$64.83m (F29), and held at zero thereafter because no further facility is evidenced. Second, section five now carries the funding question as an explicit risk with the sourced cash-flow evidence, and states the residual gap: if the benchmark falls to the guide-consistent path early the out-year cash generation thins to near nothing and no refinancing line, equity issue or asset-sale programme is evidenced beyond the half's borrowings. A bear-case financing SHOCK is not added because the method card requires mirrored shocks and no sourced downside magnitude for a financing event exists.

challenges.challenge: tax_rate 0.40 is set below the LK-implied 43.5% effective rate disclosed in the same release (PBT US$286.1m vs net US$161.8m, S3) on an unsourced 'haircut' assumption; on near-zero trough margins a 3.5pp tax understatement flatters every positive year.
challenges.answer: The unsourced haircut is gone: a.tax_rate now carries the effective rate the release implies on the group basis the model runs — pre-tax US$286.1m (F22) against net US$161.8m (F23), i.e. 43.5% — applied to positive pre-tax profit only. The 40% the red team challenged is removed, not sourced, because no withholding relief or loss-carry-forward schedule was evidenced in any reachable document. Sensitivity: the tax rate is not a top-three driver here because the model's value is concentrated in the premium years, where the pre-tax margin is widest, and the price-grid sensitivity grid in section four is applied to the benchmark rather than to tax; raising the rate further would move the target down by less than the benchmark does, and the rate now carried is already the higher, filing-consistent one.

challenges.challenge: opex_pct 0.06 is padded above the disclosed 4.8% (US$232.6m on US$4,808.8m, S3) for an unquantified 'holding-company cost layer', an unsourced conservatism that depresses value by ~US$58m a year.
challenges.answer: The pad is removed: a.opex_pct is back to the rate the filing shows — operating expenses of US$232.6m (F20) against group revenue of US$4,808.8m (F6) — with no holdco layer added, because no segment note was reachable to source one (the company IR download endpoint is captcha-gated) and the method card forbids an unsourced conservatism. The prior draft's six per cent had depressed value by tens of millions of dollars a year for an unquantified holding-company cost; the difference now lives where caution belongs, in the bear case, which loses both volume and realisation.

challenges.challenge: The group restatement is one line: only revenue FY2025A (F6) is restated while cogs, ebit, np_parent history, equity, cash, debt, capex, da and all bs_* facts are missing, so FY2024A revenue (1,359.68, narrow basis) and FY2025A (4,808.8, physical basis) sit side by side and the June balance sheet coherence is unverified; da_unit and capex_unit therefore remain S0 estimates.
challenges.answer: Both limbs taken, as far as reachable evidence allows, and the shortfall is named. (a) The FY2025A income statement is restated line by line on the group basis — revenue F6, cost of revenue F18, gross profit F19, operating expenses F20, operating profit F21, pre-tax profit F22, net profit F23 and parent net profit F10 — so revenue, cost and gross hold together on one basis. (b) The June balance sheet is now corroborated, not merely asserted: the interim disclosure gives cash US$179.68m (F28), total assets US$4.59bn (F31) and total equity US$2.95bn (F32) and all three agree with the pack's latest-balance-sheet fields, so the balance sheet needs no restatement. (c) D&A is no longer an S0 guess: it is solved from the disclosed lines — cost of revenue less the guided cash cost less the band royalty = about US$167m, 2.24 US$/t — and carried as the per-tonne input, with the calibration gate's residual gap disclosed as the pack-D&A artefact it is. (d) FY2024A cannot be restated line by line: the release states only its group revenue, gross profit, net profit and parent net profit, and a part-restatement would break the revenue-minus-cost identity, so the mixed-basis break stays flagged in section three and both leverage reads are shown. The audited notes themselves are unreachable — the IR download endpoint is captcha-gated — which is now stated as the first open item.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E base ASP of US$73.75 exceeds management's US$60-62 guide (F9) by ~21% because the deck's US$137/t benchmark carries a war premium the guide does not adopt; all positive life-DCF present value (US$268.9m) concentrates in premium years, so the base case, not the bull, prices the premium.
challenges.answer: The second limb, implemented so the red team can read it off the tables.
